# What has actually been verified

*Generated by `tools/verify/report.py` from the last run of `tools/verify/run.sh`. Do not edit by hand — re-run it instead.*

This file exists because the problem bank was written by an AI, and its authors checked each
solution against examples they had themselves written. That is self-consistency, not
correctness: a wrong solution paired with a wrong expected output agrees with itself
perfectly. What follows is what an external tool can say about the same code.

## The short version

| | |
|---|---|
| Solutions that **compile** | **165/165** |
| Solutions that **produce the answers printed on their own page** | **124/165** (0 mismatch) |
| Solutions that **agree with an independent brute force** on random legal inputs | **32/165** (0 disagree) |
| Random inputs tried in the differential stage | 12,800 |

**What none of this proves:** that a solution would pass LeetCode. The problem statements in
this library are a reconstruction, not a copy, so the *specification itself* is unverified —
a solution can be a perfect implementation of a subtly wrong problem and everything here
still goes green. Typing one into a judge remains the only way to know, which is what the
practice link on every problem page is for.

## The three checks, and what each is worth

**1. Compilation** is the broadest and shallowest. javac has no idea what the author
intended, so a block that compiles is at least valid Java with consistent types and real
library calls. Nobody had ever run it over this bank before.

**2. Example replay** runs each solution against the worked examples printed beside it. It
catches a solution that does not produce the answer its own page claims — a real failure
mode, since code and examples were written in the same sitting. It cannot catch wrongness
the examples do not exercise, which is most wrongness: three inputs chosen by the person who
wrote the code are exactly the three inputs the code was made to satisfy.

**3. Differential testing** is the strong one. Where a problem carries a runnable brute
force, the two implementations are independent programs for the same specification, run over
hundreds of random inputs drawn from the problem's own stated constraints and required to
agree exactly. For that to pass while the solution is wrong, the same mistake has to appear
twice, in two algorithms that share no structure. Its weakness is coverage:
117 problems carry a brute force written as an
excerpt rather than a program, so there is nothing to test against.

## What it found

Two genuine defects, both in **brute-force** code — which matters more than it sounds, because
the brute force is the part the reader is shown first and invited to reason about.

**`house-robber-ii`** — the enumeration treats house `i` as adjacent to `(i + 1) % n`. With a
single house that is the house itself, so it appeared to be its own neighbour and every plan
was rejected: `rob([9])` returned 0 where the constraints say plainly that "a single house is
trivially legal". The optimised solution had the `n == 1` case carved out and was right all
along; the two disagreed on the first trial. Fixed, and the case added to that problem's
common mistakes, because it is the trap any wrap-around adjacency sets.

**`number-of-operations-to-connect`** — the brute force counted how many cables were
individually redundant, removing each from the *original* graph. That overcounts: a triangle
has three individually-redundant edges but only one genuine spare, since pulling all three
collapses it. On 6 computers and 3 cables it reported 3 moves where the answer is -1, because
6 computers cannot be connected with fewer than 5 cables at all. Fixed by testing each cable
against what is left rather than against the original.

Both were found by the differential stage, and neither would have been found by the example
replay — the examples on both pages passed throughout.

## Where the harness had to be told the rules

The first differential run reported fourteen failures and not one was a defect. They were
inputs the problems forbid: negative prices fed to a problem constrained to `0 <= prices[i]`,
empty arrays given to one that says `1 <= nums.length`, values outside `{0,1,2}` handed to
sort-colors. An implementation owes no sensible behaviour outside its stated domain, and a
report full of such findings teaches the reader to ignore it.

So the generator reads each problem's own `constraints` list — 165
problems, of which the parser understands the stated domain for those written as ranges. A
handful state *structural* preconditions no type-driven generator will hit by chance ("every
element appears exactly twice except one", "the grid is a permutation of 0..n²−1", "both
arrays are already sorted"); those have named repairs in `tools/verify/src/Preconditions.java`,
each quoting the constraint it enforces. Two problems say their answer may be returned in any
order, and that flag is read from their statements rather than assumed.

## Running it yourself

```
./tools/verify/run.sh          # extract, compile, replay examples, differential test
python3 tools/verify/report.py # rewrite this document from the results
```

It exits non-zero if any solution fails to compile, contradicts its own page, or disagrees
with its brute force, so it belongs in CI if this ever gets one.
